transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-12-05 15:00 UTC
Duration: 63 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Lina Park (Redwood AE), Gabe Ortiz (Redwood SE), Priya Sharma (CTO, Horizon Labs), Marcus Leung (Head of Platform), Elena Petrov (Security Engineer), Tomás Rios (DevOps), Sofia Kim (Compliance)

Summary:
Quick architecture deep-dive focused on network segmentation for private deployment, ingress/egress controls, firewall posture, KMS/integration and key provenance to satisfy SOC 2/ISO expectations. Outcome: Redwood to share docs and follow-up with a technical working session.

Topics Covered:
- VPC vs on-prem network zoning and isolation
- Ingress patterns, private control plane, and bastion/management plane
- Egress locks, proxy design, and logging/audit collection
- Encryption key lifecycle: KMS, HSM, rotation, split keys, provenance
- RBAC/SSO mapping and audit log retention for compliance

Transcript body:
[00:00] Lina Park: Hi everyone thanks for joining, I'm Lina from Redwood, I think we have about an hour, we'll try to cover both the network zoning stuff and then deep dive into key management since that was flagged in your RFP.
[00:08] Priya Sharma: Morning — actually afternoon for some of us — thanks, we want to make sure the private deployment fits our SOC two and ISO controls, especially around key provenance and egress.
[00:16] Gabe Ortiz: Great, I'll start with a quick sketch of the control plane layout, then we can hop into firewall and KMS. Apologies in advance if the network diagram in the notes has a small typo, my VPN's being weird.
[00:26] Marcus Leung: No worries, go ahead.
[00:30] Gabe Ortiz: Okay so on Redwood Private there are two logical planes: the customer data plane that runs in your VPC or on-prem cluster, and a lightweight control plane which can be either customer-hosted or hosted by Redwood depending on the model. For Horizon's case you mentioned wanting a fully customer-managed control plane — is that right, Priya?
[00:45] Priya Sharma: Correct, we need the control plane to live in our environment. We can't have call-home for secrets — all keys must sit behind our KMS.
[00:52] Lina Park: Understood. For that we support an on-prem control plane deployment with customer-managed KMS, and an air-gapped option if needed. It requires a small set of egress rules for updates if you opt into Redwood-managed components, but you can also opt for full airgap and we provide signed bundles.
[01:09] Elena Petrov: When you say KMS, are we talking cloud KMS integrations or an HSM appliance? We need to know if Redwood supports BYOK into an HSM and how key provenance is preserved.
[01:20] Gabe Ortiz: Yes both — we integrate with cloud KMS (AWS KMS, Google KMS, Azure Key Vault) and also with on-prem HSMs via a KMS proxy. For provenance, we store a signed certificate chain of key usage events and tie them back to audit logs. Quick caveat: in the transcript the word "K-V cash" sometimes shows up, but it's KV cache — not relevant to keys.
[01:43] Tomás Rios: Can you explain rotation flows? Our compliance requires quarterly rotation and a strong audit trail showing key ancestry when secrets are rewrapped.
[01:52] Gabe Ortiz: Rotation is supported two ways: automated rotation where the Redwood agent rewraps material using your KMS and records the operation in the audit log, and manual rotation where you push a new wrapping key. Each rewrap event includes a signed manifest with time, operator identity, and a reference to the prior key fingerprint — that satisfies lineage/provenance needs.
[02:12] Sofia Kim: How do you guarantee non-repudiation? We need to prove that no unauthorized key material was used during a period.
[02:19] Gabe Ortiz: We do a couple things: 1) all agent operations are signed by a machine identity tied to your cluster and recorded to an append-only audit log; 2) the log is shipped to your SIEM or to a customer-managed object store with write-once permissions; 3) optional HSM signing for highest assurance.
[02:35] Priya Sharma: About the audit log retention — SOC 2 usually expects a year of retention for certain artifacts. Does Redwood support configurable retention windows and export to our S3?
[02:45] Lina Park: Yes, logs can be configured for retention and automatic export. For Private deployments, logs never go to Redwood unless you enable a managed collection; default is local-only and you push to your compliance tier.
[02:58] Marcus Leung: Network side question: our security team wants strict egress controls — essentially only allow traffic to our internal update mirror and an egress proxy for telemetry. How does Redwood handle offline updates?
[03:09] Gabe Ortiz: We support signed update packages that you can pull into an internal mirror. For telemetry you can route to your egress proxy; we also support push-to-s3 patterns where the agent only writes to an internal store. There's no mandatory phone-home.
[03:23] Elena Petrov: Good. For firewall rules, what's the minimum set of ports required for the control plane and nodes to talk? We need to document it for our firewall policy.
[03:33] Gabe Ortiz: Minimum is typically 443 outbound for TLS to your mirror; 22 only if you enable SSH bastion access — otherwise management is via an API over mTLS. For internal node-to-node we use high ports for gRPC and a health port, but those can be locked to a CIDR range. I'll drop a spreadsheet with the exact port list.
[03:50] Tomás Rios: Can we lock Node API traffic to private subnets only? We don't want any public IPs.
[03:55] Lina Park: Absolutely — private IP only is supported. In fact most enterprise customers run in private subnets behind NAT with no public IPs.
[04:03] Priya Sharma: On RBAC, we have complex org roles — platform, data science, product — and need mapping from our SSO (SAML) to RBAC in the control plane. How granular is the RBAC model?
[04:14] Gabe Ortiz: RBAC is role-based with resource scoping down to model routes and environment names. You can map SAML groups to roles and also apply attribute-based rules for environment scoping. There is an audit trail for role grants. There are some limits on dynamic attributes but the mapping covers most enterprise setups.
[04:33] Elena Petrov: Any gotchas on SAML? For example, DoS of assertion replay or token lifetimes?
[04:39] Gabe Ortiz: We validate assertion replay with nonce and short assertion lifetimes and also log every token exchange. If you want an additional layer we support mTLS client certs for service identities.
[04:50] [00:05:00] Priya Sharma: We need to dig into key provenance more — show me an example of the audit event that proves a key was used to wrap a token.
[05:06] Gabe Ortiz: Sure, verbally: it's a JSON manifest containing the time, the operation type (wrap/unwrap/rotate), the key fingerprint (SHA256), the actor (service account or operator), the cluster identity, and a signature from the HSM or agent identity.
[05:22] Priya Sharma: Would that be sufficient for our external auditor? They want chain of custody for crypto ops.
[05:28] Sofia Kim: Our auditors will ask for chain of custody plus proof keys weren't exported.
[05:34] Lina Park: The HSM-backed flow prevents export of roots; for cloud KMS there's a clear role separation — Redwood has no plaintext key access if you configure envelope encryption where customer root never leaves KMS. We can demonstrate this in a short runbook.
[05:48] Marcus Leung: About envelope encryption — what parts of the data are encrypted at rest? Models, KV cache, temp swap?
[05:56] Gabe Ortiz: Everything persistently stored on disk in the data plane is encrypted at rest via the customer-controlled KMS. KV cache in memory isn't persisted by default, but if you enable sharding or swap it can be rewrapped on disk. We'll provide recommended op flags to avoid swap.
[06:13] Tomás Rios: Does Redwood's runtime ever write model shards to NFS or shared storage that we don't control?
[06:19] Gabe Ortiz: No, model shards are stored on your block storage. For Dedicated we manage the storage but for Private it's yours.
[06:25] Elena Petrov: Ok. Moving back to network segmentation — we'd like segmentation between model hosting, admin tools, and telemetry. Can Redwood support microsegmentation or host-level firewalls?
[06:36] Gabe Ortiz: Yes, you can apply iptables-level host firewalls via init scripts and we offer network policies for k8s deployments. We also support strict CNI enforcement at the pod-level for on-prem.
[06:47] Priya Sharma: If we enable host firewalling does Redwood need any special privileges? We're sensitive about granting cluster-admin.
[06:53] Lina Park: We operate with least privilege. For on-prem install we request a namespaced service account and ephemeral privileges for install which are revoked after bootstrap. We document the exact K8s RBAC verbs required.
[07:06] [00:10:00] Marcus Leung: Let's talk egress proxy design. Our security team prefers a forced egress proxy with TLS inspection. Does Redwood support proxy chaining and certificate pinning?
[07:18] Gabe Ortiz: We support upstream proxies and can pin server certs for update endpoints. For telemetry, we recommend mutual TLS between agent and egress proxy and we can configure the agent to use a proxy with basic auth or mTLS.
[07:30] Tomás Rios: When using TLS inspection, does the agent expose plaintext to local processes? Concern is local admin seeing secrets.
[07:38] Gabe Ortiz: The agent never exposes unencrypted key material to other processes; decryption occurs in-process within the isolation boundary and keys are never written to shared procfs. There's an option to use a secure enclave for extra protection.
[07:51] Elena Petrov: Secure enclaves — are you referring to SGX or an HSM?
[07:54] Gabe Ortiz: Could be SGX or an HSM-backed enclave. We have some customers using Nitro Enclaves on AWS as an added protection for inference secrets.
[08:04] Priya Sharma: Data residency — our product teams in EU require that logs and models do not leave EU regions. How do you ensure that?
[08:12] Lina Park: For Private deployments you choose the data plane region — logs and artifacts stay within your infra. If you choose Redwood-hosted components we can pin them to a region or opt out of cross-region backups.
[08:24] Sofia Kim: On compliance, do you have SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 certs we can reference?
[08:30] Lina Park: Yes — we'll share the most recent SOC 2 and ISO artifacts. Note that some evidence is redacted; for full auditor access we typically execute an NDA and a controls review.
[08:42] [00:15:00] Priya Sharma: One question on secret promotion: our CI creates tokens that are then consumed by model-serving nodes. We need an approval step with an auditable workflow. Can Redwood integrate with our CI and require operator approval prior to promotion?
[08:55] Gabe Ortiz: Yes, you can configure an approval webhook or require an X-of-Y sign-off via your ticketing system. All approvals become audit events.
[09:06] Marcus Leung: On the topic of service accounts, can we map their lifetime and require short-lived credentials?
[09:12] Gabe Ortiz: Short-lived creds are supported; we recommend short TTLs for service tokens and automatic rotation via the agent.
[09:18] Elena Petrov: Any details on sealing/unsealing the node when it reboots? We need to ensure keys aren't left unsealed after restart.
[09:25] Gabe Ortiz: Nodes require a bootstrap workflow that obtains a transient unseal token from your KMS and then rewraps the node-key; you can require manual operator involvement for extra assurance.
[09:36] [00:20:00] Tomás Rios: Let's talk firewall and port hygiene again — do you publish a single manifest we can hand to infra?
[09:44] Gabe Ortiz: Yes I'll attach a minimal firewall manifest with exact CIDRs and ports; it's standard in our runbook.
[09:50] Priya Sharma: For the auditor, we need a demonstration of a rewrap event — could we do a live demo in the follow-up?
[09:56] Lina Park: Absolutely. Suggest we do a 30–45 minute demo with your security engineer. We'll show a rewrap from a test key and the resulting audit artifacts.
[10:06] Elena Petrov: Make sure the demo includes the signed manifest and where it's pushed.
[10:10] Gabe Ortiz: Will do.
[10:12] [00:25:00] Marcus Leung: Regarding partitioning access: can we have separate tenants in the same cluster for different product orgs, with network segmentation between them?
[10:22] Gabe Ortiz: Multi-tenant patterns are supported via namespace isolation, network policies, and per-namespace RBAC. We recommend dedicated node pools to strengthen isolation.
[10:31] Tomás Rios: If one tenant misbehaves can we auto-quarantine?
[10:35] Gabe Ortiz: Yes, we offer admission webhook policies to deny or throttle workloads and an automated quarantine flow that isolates the namespace and revokes its service tokens.
[10:44] Priya Sharma: On the topic of log integrity, can you write logs to WORM storage or to our SIEM with signed checksums?
[10:53] Gabe Ortiz: Yes, logs can be pushed to WORM buckets or archived with SHA256 checksums and signatures; we also support streaming to SIEMs with a signed sequence number for tamper detection.
[11:03] [00:30:00] Elena Petrov: Any limitations around large model downloads crossing egress controls? For example, our models are hundreds of GBs — we want the control plane to orchestrate fetches and not the nodes reaching out directly to external endpoints.
[11:16] Gabe Ortiz: For large artifacts we recommend using an internal artifact mirror. The control plane can orchestrate fetches via the mirror and we provide hooks to pause or validate artifacts before serving.
[11:27] Marcus Leung: On the topic of encryption in transit, do you support per-connection mTLS with client certs issued by our PKI?
[11:34] Gabe Ortiz: Yes, we support mTLS with your PKI for all inter-node and control plane traffic.
[11:39] Tomás Rios: A practical question: how much increased latency does envelope encryption add for inference?
[11:44] Gabe Ortiz: Negligible for token paths — envelope unwrap is only during load/initialization. At inference time keys are cached in memory in a secure boundary with a very small overhead. We'll provide numbers in the follow-up benchmark doc.
[11:57] [00:35:00] Priya Sharma: Competitors question: we looked at Anthropic and OpenAI integrations — what are the main differences from a security posture perspective?
[12:04] Lina Park: Without naming too much, Redwood's Private option focuses on giving you full control of the data plane and KMS integration, whereas some hosted-only APIs don't offer BYOK or on-prem deployments; we'll share a short comparison doc.
[12:15] Sofia Kim: For the external auditor we may need a signed consensus on the control mapping; is Redwood willing to participate in an auditor call?
[12:22] Lina Park: Yes we regularly join auditor calls under NDA. We'll coordinate scheduling after you review the SOC artifacts.
[12:30] [00:40:00] Elena Petrov: Corner cases — what happens during partial upgrades? We want to ensure no drift leaves nodes in an inconsistent state that could bypass controls.
[12:41] Gabe Ortiz: Upgrades are orchestrated with canaries and health gates; the bootstrap verifies control-plane compat before promoting. We also run a post-upgrade verification suite that checks network policies and key access controls.
[12:54] Marcus Leung: About secret scanning — will Redwood's logs expose secret values inadvertently?
[13:01] Gabe Ortiz: No, logs redact secrets by default. We also support PII/secret scanning rules before log export to ensure nothing sensitive is persisted.
[13:12] [00:45:00] Priya Sharma: For compliance evidence generation, can Redwood produce an artifact bundle for auditors with redaction options?
[13:21] Lina Park: Yes, we can produce a controls evidence bundle with configurable redaction and a signed manifest of included files.
[13:29] Tomás Rios: Any recommendations for KMS key policies to prevent rogue rotations?
[13:36] Gabe Ortiz: Use least-privilege key policies, deny putKeyPolicy to general admins, require an approval step for rotation and require HSM wrapping for root keys. We'll share a policy template.
[13:47] Elena Petrov: On HSM integration — do you support PKCS#11 or vendor-specific APIs?
[13:52] Gabe Ortiz: We support PKCS#11 and vendor SDKs; for some appliances we use a local proxy to normalize calls.
[13:59] [00:50:00] Sofia Kim: Are there any documented incidents or caveats we should be aware of for private deployments?
[14:05] Lina Park: We maintain a public changelog and responsible disclosure history. For private deployments, most incidents are misconfiguration-related and our runbooks cover those. We'll share a summary document.
[14:15] Priya Sharma: From the compliance team side, we'll want a runbook for breach response that maps to our IR plan. Can Redwood align on SLAs for incident response?
[14:24] Lina Park: We offer incident response SLAs in enterprise contracts. For private deployments we can agree on response times and blameless post-mortems.
[14:34] [00:55:00] Marcus Leung: A couple of last quick things: 1) Can we get a list of exact API endpoints that need to be whitelisted for the install? 2) Sample terraform or helm charts?
[14:44] Gabe Ortiz: Yes to both. We'll add a terraform/helm sample repo link.
[14:50] Priya Sharma: Great. Any more questions from Horizon team?
[14:53] Elena Petrov: Not right now — we'll digest and come back with a prioritized checklist.
[14:58] Tomás Rios: We'll want the follow-up demo in our staging cluster.
[15:02] Lina Park: Sounds good. We'll send calendar invites and the SOC/ISO pack. Thanks everyone.
[15:08] Priya Sharma: Thanks all.

Recap (verbatim notes):
- Redwood supports on-prem and customer-managed control plane with BYOK/HSM integration and signed key provenance manifests.
- Logs can be kept local, pushed to customer S3, or archived to WORM storage; signed checksums supported.
- Firewall manifest and port list to be provided; private subnets-only supported.
- RBAC maps from SAML groups; short-lived service tokens supported.
- Egress proxy and TLS inspection patterns supported; telemetry can be routed through customer proxy.
- Follow-up: demo of key rewrap + runbook and technical workshop on egress proxy.

End of transcript.
